1000503.etyen: Borrowed from English Mars (“Mars, Pennsylvania”). The origin of the English place name is disputed. In 1873, Samuel Parks established a local post office with the help of Samuel Marshall. According to the borough's official history, one tradition says that Parks's wife, who was interested in astronomy, suggested the name, while another says that it honoured Samuel Marshall; the latter is described as the prevailing local view. The name was later also adopted for the railway stop, replacing Overbrook.

1001015.etyen:

The first element continues Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”). The deeper origin of κέλαδος (kélados) is unclear; a connection with Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”) has been proposed, but is considered problematic because the expected Greek vocalism would be different.

1004343.etyen:
An old Norwegian river name, usually connected with the reconstructed Germanic stems *swark- and *swork- (“to darken, become black”), related to svart (“black”); hence probably originally “the dark one”. A sound-symbolic origin, comparable to surkle (“to gurgle”), has also been proposed.
Compare the related Norwegian river names Svarka, Sverka and Svorka.
First attested in the Middle Ages indirectly in Surkudalr, the Old Norse name of Sørkedalen.

1004599.etyen:
The first element is unknown; the final element continues Old Norse nes (“headland, promontory”). Oluf Rygh tentatively connected the first element with the old district name Jessum in Ullensaker, represented by Old Norse Jaseimr and Jesseimr, but noted that other possible explanations were incompatible with the early form.
First attested in 1346 as Jæsnes.
